#600. ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Producer Alex Gayner Thought He’d Solved Every Problem a Set Could Throw at Him. Then Came a Runaway Parrot.

Ten seconds of footage ended up being the most nerve-wracking part of the shoot for the movie veteran who has been on sets since the '90s.

Filmmakers often thrive on controlled chaos. Alex Gayner has spent his career orchestrating that madness.

Long before producing The Mosquito Bowl for Peter Berg, Gayner cut his teeth doing odd jobs on ’90s direct-to-video actioners — the kind of movies you’d stumble across on a pay-cable channel at 1 AM during a bout of insomnia. Then, a second assistant director was let go before lunch, and Gayner found himself promoted on the spot. It was an unlikely break that set the course for the rest of his career.

He gradually climbed the ranks to first assistant director, eventually trading B-movies for some of the biggest studio productions around, including Guillermo del Toro’s Pacific Rim and Gareth Edwards’ Godzilla. He also developed a reputation as a closer, overseeing reshoots for Suicide Squad (2016), Birds of Prey, Zero Dark Thirty and Mulan, among others. Related Stories TV 'Beef' Creator Lee Sung Jin Launches Production Company, Plans Ali Wong Limited Series Movies Ray Nicholson Levels Up With 'The Mosquito Bowl': "I'm Always Battling for Legitimacy"

Another turning point arrived in the late 2010s, when the native New Yorker decided to pivot to producing. If the first AD is the on-set quarterback who executes the plays on the field, then Gayner wanted to become a full-time offensive coordinator, the person drawing up the plays and mapping out the production behind the scenes.

He credits Nicolas Winding Refn with giving him his big break as a producer on the 2019 limited series Too Old to Die Young, an opportunity that paved the way for him to produce the first season of Beef and win an Emmy for his work. (Gayner and Refn are now assembling the latter’s long-gestating Maniac Cop reimagining, which recently received approval for a California tax credit.)

After wrapping Beef, Netflix pointed Gayner toward Berg’s 19th-century Western limited series American Primeval. But first, the two had to bridge the gap between the producer Berg expected and the one Gayner turned out to be.

“When I met Pete, I don’t think he really knew what kind of producer I was,” Gayner tells The Hollywood Reporter. “Naturally, he didn’t know if I was going to come in to watch the money or try to make the show on soundstages. We had to figure each other out.”

To keep the football metaphors going, Berg likes to run his sets with a no-huddle offense, frequently calling audibles along the way. He might improvise dialogue, change camera positions or throw out the playbook altogether. Most of all, he has a strict devotion to immersive, practical filmmaking. Fortunately, Gayner has been adapting on the fly ever since that lunchtime promotion more than 30 years ago. He also shares Berg’s preference for capturing as much as possible in camera.

Thus, they quickly got on the same page for American Primeval, setting the stage for two features, The Mosquito Bowl and the highly anticipated Call of Duty video game adaptation.

“That [adherence to practical] really solidified our relationship as filmmaking partners. He knew I wasn’t afraid to go back to the old-school way of how we learned to do things,” Gayner says. “It’s a little uncomfortable to get that realism and that immersive, visceral experience on film, but it’s worth pushing the envelope.”

The Mosquito Bowl, based on a novel by Berg’s cousin Buzz Bissinger, chronicles four real-life college football players who enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps during World War II and played in a fabled 1944 football game known as the Mosquito Bowl alongside 60 other former collegiate players turned soldiers.

Berg and Gayner threw Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis into football crash courses with help from San Francisco 49ers All-Pro running back Christian McCaffrey, the New York Giants and two of the industry’s best on-set football coordinators. Then they dropped the actors into the ocean and jungle of Queensland, Australia, doubling for Japan, while surrounding them with tanks, explosions, flamethrowers and blank gunfire.

Berg wanted to honor one specific character detail that belonged to Nicholson’s Tony Butkovich, the former Purdue University fullback who was drafted in the first round by the NFL’s Cleveland Rams prior to enlistment. Bissinger wrote about how Butkovich sent photos home of himself with a parrot on his shoulder, so Gayner received the unenviable task of tracking down what would become the one-and-only available parrot on the island continent. But the bird was still young, and its wings had to be clipped to prevent catastrophe during filming.

After months of planning and training, cameras finally rolled on Nicholson and the supposedly grounded parrot. Within seconds, the parrot flew off into the 100-foot-tall trees. Its four wranglers panicked, as did the rest of the stunned cast and crew. Gayner, meanwhile, tried to counter Berg’s fatalism with optimism.

“Pete looked at me and said, ‘I know exactly what’s going to happen. The headline of every entertainment paper in L.A. is going to be, “Peter Berg Kills Parrot During Filming of The Mosquito Bowl.”’ And I said, ‘No, Pete, we’re going to find the parrot.’”

Hours later, they managed to retrieve the parrot from a tree and tie a string to its leg as an added precaution until they got the necessary shots. The trial amounted to roughly ten seconds of footage in the final cut, but it’s a stark reminder of how much labor goes into even the briefest moments on screen.

“We can control actors, special effects and stunts. But when the only parrot in Australia that’s available for our movie flies away, you’re stuck,” Gayner says. “We didn’t want to use a CG parrot. We’d made that commitment.”

Below, in a conversation with THR, Gayner elaborates on training two British actors and a Swedish actor to play a sport they’d never played before, let alone understood.

Your filmography is overwhelming. You’ve seen some things, haven’t you?

(Laughs.) I’ve seen a few things, yeah. I’ve been around the block. I’ve gone from tiny little things to big giant things — and everything in between.

I can only imagine the war stories you must have, especially as first assistant director. That’s widely considered the most stressful job on set. First ADs are often regarded as the quarterback to the director’s head coach. Did you have any kind of support group with your fellow first ADs?

Not really, because first ADs never work with other first ADs. You can talk to each other, share experiences and discuss your approaches to working with directors, but you never really get to spend time with them, especially on a movie set, unless there’s a first and second unit. Everybody has such different styles. But it is a stressful job. It’s a heavy-lifting job.

I started making films in Hollywood when I was 20 years old, and I worked for a very low-budget film company that made straight-to-video action movies. They filmed one movie every three weeks. So we would do 18-day shoots — three consecutive six-day weeks — with the exact same crew. We’d wrap a movie on a Friday, and then we’d start a new movie on a Monday. You’d get the script midway through one movie, and everybody would just roll onto the next film. I did that for three years, and I made 30 films in three years.

I did everything from driving the grip truck to learning how to load film, because we were still shooting film at the time, to being a boom person and working with the grips and the electric. So it really was my film school, and it taught me so much about what everybody does on a film set. Then I just happened to fall into the AD department because a second AD got let go. At lunch, they were like, “Alright, you’re now the second 2nd.” And I was like, “Okay, I’ll figure out how to do that.” Eventually, that happened with the [first] AD.

Why do you think these assistant director roles fit you so well?

I have a knack for communicating with all the departments and rallying everybody to have a common vision. And as I started to become a first AD on smaller movies before eventually doing some second-unit action sequences and working my way up to the bigger studio films, I made it less stressful for myself. I really understood what everybody was up against and what everybody was doing. I didn’t want to live under that constant pressure of only being focused on, How are we going to make our day? How are we going to get the schedule done? We have to just keep going.

That is part of the job, but really, I’m a filmmaker. I want to participate creatively in supporting the story and the characters. And as a first AD, if you can figure out how to do your job and motivate the crew — while working in a respectful environment with a couple hundred people, keeping them on the same page and being a good creative partner to the director, the producer and the studio — it takes a lot of the pressure off. You’re not being this machine butting up against an artist trying to birth something that’s in their brain.

So, as a first AD, I was always a creative first, and I figured out how to translate that into the schedule, the days, the shot lists and the time that the DP had to light. Integrating myself as a creative partner to everybody made it less stressful and more enjoyable.

Another pattern in your work is that you tend to assistant-direct a lot of additional photography. Examples include: Suicide Squad, Birds of Prey, Zero Dark Thirty, Mulan and Total Recall. That’s a fraught period of time since the production is spending the last of its money, and there’s a lot riding on the additions and/or revisions. Was there a reason why your number kept getting called for reshoots? Are you the Winston Wolf of reshoots?

(Laughs.) I don’t really know the answer. Part of it was schedule and circumstance. Another part of it was word of mouth. I really took pride in what I did as a first AD, and I’m a very even, mild-mannered first AD. There are some who are not. Everybody has their own style, but I always was very balanced and very calm in the pocket, so to speak, to go back to your quarterback reference. So I think that reputation just got around town.

Also, if a director’s usual first AD wasn’t available for reshoots, I tended to be on the short list to be called. It was very flattering. It was a really great way to build relationships with other directors without having to commit a year or two to the overall process, and it expanded my résumé quite a bit.

You’d produced here and there prior to 2023, but did your Emmy for producing Beef season one lead you to produce full-time? It looks like you stopped assistant-directing that same year.

I’d been going back and forth before producing Beef. The last movie I AD’d was Spiderhead with Joe Kosinski during COVID. It was a very hard transition. I’d worked so long to be successful as an AD, and then I looked in the mirror and went, “Alright, I’m going to stop doing this and make the transition to producer.” With a family and a mortgage, it was a big commitment to step into a new role, essentially starting at the bottom. But I knew that it was the natural next step, something I had to do and really wanted to do. The project that got me really confident as a producer was a limited series called Too Old to Die Young that Nicolas Winding Refn directed.

Big fan. Every time I see Nell Tiger Free, I remind her how haunting her beach scene with Miles Teller is.

I absolutely remember that day. We went up to the [Mugu] rock at the end of Malibu, right on the turn there. It was a wild show, and I loved making it. Nick originally called me to AD the series, and I turned him down because I was really committed to producing. But he kept calling me and calling me. And I said, “Nick, look, I really appreciate it, but I have to stick to this. I have to make this transition. This is what I’m going to do.” In 2017, limited series really weren’t that big a thing yet, and Amazon, under Roy Price, was also still finding its legs. This was long before Jen Salke came in.

Then Nick said, “I’ll tell you what, I’m going to direct this entire series by myself, which I’ve never done before. If you AD the first episode of the show for me, I’d love for you to produce the series. Once you get me on my feet, then you can produce the rest of the episodes. I just need you to prep for me and help me with casting and finding locations.”

So we figured out what would work for him and what would work for me, and we made a deal. I AD’d the first three weeks or so, and then I stepped off the set. Other ADs then came in, and I produced the rest of the show. Nick wrote the series with Ed Brubaker, and besides directing all the episodes, he was editing every night. So he was at it seven days a week, 20 hours a day.

It was a fantastic experience and one of the most creative things I’ve ever been a part of. It was such a specific vision that he had. We shot most of it in L.A. over a hundred days. It was a very small-budget show, and we stretched every dollar. That was really the beginning of producing for me.

Do you think Maniac Cop is ever going to happen?

I’m as sure as I can be. It just qualified for the California Tax Credit. It got approved. He’s making it as a film instead of a series. We tried to make it as a series for HBO. We were very close to making it, but once COVID hit, it was just impossible to make that kind of show at the time.

You wrapped Beef season one in 2022. In 2023, you EP’d American Primeval for Pete Berg. Did you hit it off to such a degree that he wanted you to be his boots-on-the-ground producer and UPM for The Mosquito Bowl?

American Primeval was a very complicated show to make out in the elements for a hundred-plus days. I was asked to come in as a non-writing EP. Pete and I had never worked together. I’d never even met him. I had previously worked with the other executive producer, Eric Newman, and I had a longstanding relationship with a lot of people at Netflix.

When I met Pete, I don’t think he really knew what kind of producer I was. He’s worked with a lot of the same people over the years, and he has this very raw, immersive, visceral vision of whatever he’s making. So, naturally, he didn’t know if I was going to come in to watch the money or try to make the show on soundstages. We had to figure each other out.

But as soon as we hit the ground in New Mexico, he learned that I have the same desire to make films and television as practically as he does. There are definitely benefits to going on stage and shooting blue screen for certain pieces, but for a huge sequence at the end that takes place on top of a snowy mountain, there was talk of going to a quarry-type setting and making fake snow in a very controlled environment. As soon as I started talking creatively with Pete about it, I knew there was no way this was going to work for what he was trying to do visually and what Mark L. Smith wrote.

My first reaction and suggestion to that proposed plan was, “I don’t want to do that. I want to gather a lean crew with as little gear as possible, and climb up a mountain in the real snow. We can build a shack and do it for real, while having access and keeping everybody as safe and comfortable as humanly possible.” To fabricate all that in the New Mexico summer and then add visual effects, it would’ve felt too different. Paper snow doesn’t react to horses the same way as real snow, and that went for every element of that sequence.

So that [adherence to practical filmmaking] really solidified our relationship as filmmaking partners. He knew I wasn’t afraid to go back to the old-school way of how we learned to do things. It’s a little uncomfortable to get that realism and that immersive, visceral experience on film, but it’s worth pushing the envelope.

Pete is known for having a very vocal, energetic and off-the-cuff directing style. He’ll throw out alternate dialogue mid-take without cutting. How did you adapt your own process to his “no-huddle” manner of shooting a movie?

I didn’t have to adapt that much. Working with Pete as a producer, it’s like creating an action-packed play. He’s very improvisational. If something comes to mind on set, he goes for it. Being a First AD for so many different kinds of directors, as well as shooting additional photography, really served me as a producer. I learned how to step into a preexisting structure, whether for a couple of scenes or a whole sequence, and adapt to a crew that’s already been through battle together. As a producer, I try to be as responsible for the active environment I’m creating as I am for the story.

Pete especially likes a 360-degree environment, and that’s how I approach every project. There’s no cheating. You can’t go out to a location with all your trucks lined up behind you and say, “Okay, you can only look west.” That 360 approach really slimmed everything down, allowing us to be nimble and giving Pete the freedom to say, “Okay, I want to turn around and look the opposite way.” It helped us discover some magic on American Primeval and The Mosquito Bowl. Organic pieces of the puzzle fell into place. The actors appreciated it, too.

Mosquito Bowl has numerous war and football sequences, which must have been a logistical nightmare. You weren’t the First AD on this set, but that experience must have also served you well here.

100 percent. Every challenging project I’ve produced has been made better by my experience and the tools I gained as a first AD. The Mosquito Bowl wasn’t a logistical nightmare, but it was very challenging logistically. There were so many challenges to figure out on a daily basis that I had to use every tool in my toolbox.

When Pete started writing and talking about The Mosquito Bowl while we were shooting American Primeval, we agreed that if we were going to make a war movie, we had to do something different. So many amazing World War II films have already been made. We had to take responsibility for trying to capture even 0.1 percent of what these soldiers went through emotionally. Obviously, we would never compare what we do as filmmakers to what any soldier experienced in war, but we had to deliver something immersive, violent and shocking for the audience while remaining true to what really happened.

That meant putting the actors in the ocean instead of in a water tank or a pool and using real explosions and blank gunfire instead of visual effects. We had to find running tanks and develop hundred-foot flamethrowers. As a producer, I was never going to let “it’s impossible” come out of my mouth. There was always going to be a way to make it as real as possible, and that became our mission statement from the beginning.

With every person we interviewed and every department we approached about joining The Mosquito Bowl, we said, “This is how we want to do it. We want to make this as real as possible. Can you do this? Are you up for it? And what are your ideas to help us get there?”

Did San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey consult you guys as far as how to train the actors to look like capable football players in just four weeks?

He absolutely did. Christian McCaffrey helped us build the foundation for the actors to become football players. Pete, who’s friendly with Christian, gave him a call once we had Nicholas Galatzine, Bill Skarsgård, Tom Francis and Ray Nicholson on board. Christian is a beast. He’s one of the most amazing football players there is, and he’s such a gracious guy. He does so much work with veterans, and he’s involved with a nonprofit, so he was immediately willing to donate his time. He was even coming back from an injury at the time, but two days after Pete called him, he was on the field in Westlake with Ray, running plays, teaching him moves and consulting as a running back. Additionally, we sent Tom Francis to the New York Giants because he was doing Sunset Boulevard on Broadway, so he got to train with them.

We had two Brits, a Swede and one American, and with Ray being the American, he was the only one who had ever really played football. He played high school football and knew a lot about the game, but Nick, Tom and Bill didn’t know much about it. So they worked tirelessly with our football coordinators, Mike Fisher and Don Powers, who have worked on a lot of football movies. They came down to Australia and ran a four-week camp with the actors, bringing in a ton of Aussie rules football and rugby players, as well as a few college football players from the States to fill in at quarterback.

For all the football and battle sequences, ten seconds of a parrot interacting with Ray’s character was the task that put you through your paces the most?

(Laughs.) That put Pete through his paces more than anything else on the movie. I don’t know about myself. Every single day, my brain was working at a hundred miles an hour trying to solve problems. Birds and animals in Australia are different from those in other parts of the world. You have some of the deadliest snakes and spiders, as well as bull sharks. Everywhere you go, you have to be aware of nature’s pitfalls. So finding movie animals there was difficult, and Australia doesn’t have every breed you might find in North America or elsewhere.

Ray’s character, Tony Butkovich, really had a parrot as a pet during World War II. That was based on real information. But finding a movie-trained parrot that looked the way we wanted was nearly impossible. We worked with animal wranglers who eventually found one, but it was very young. They had to train it so we could feed it.

They also clipped its swings so it wouldn’t fly away. We had to shoot the scene within a specific window before the parrot got old enough to learn how to fly. So we were up against the deadline of the parrot instinctively knowing how to fly. We also shot the whole movie in continuity, so our first AD, Andrew Ward, had to figure out how to fit the scene into that window.

There had been months of logistical planning and training, and Ray had to understand what he could and couldn’t do with it. Eventually, the day came when we had to work with the parrot. We were in the jungle, surrounded by smoke. Everyone was carrying guns and wearing all this gear, but everything had to be silent and still.

Gosh, all this for ten seconds of footage.

Yeah, when Ray sat down to do the scene, the set had to be cleared. Pete couldn’t call action, and nobody could say a word. The animal wranglers put the parrot down next to Ray and made hand signals for the cameras to start rolling. Ray started feeding the parrot, and within two seconds, it flew off into the jungle. (Laughs.) The parrot that wasn’t supposed to be able to fly with its clipped wings disappeared up into the trees.

The animal wranglers freaked out, and we all had to stop and look up. We were looking for a tiny parrot in the Australian jungle, surrounded by hundred-foot trees and dense foliage. The animal wranglers then crawled through the jungle, making parrot noises and trying to call it back.

Pete looked at me and said, “I know exactly what’s going to happen. The headline of every entertainment paper in L.A is going to be, ‘Peter Berg Kills Parrot During Filming of The Mosquito Bowl.’” And I said, “No, Pete, we’re going to find the parrot.” So the search went on for hours, and the animal wranglers stacked ladders and held pool cues with baskets on the ends. Eventually, the parrot came back and we got the shots, but it was one of the most stressful ordeals.

We can control actors, special effects and stunts. We can have that kind of input. But when the only parrot in Australia that’s available for our movie flies away, you’re stuck. We didn’t want to use a CG parrot. We’d made that commitment.

You just proved why I’m endlessly fascinated by behind-the-scenes stories. Of all the projects you’ve been a part of, which one deserves the I Play Rocky treatment?

It’s between American Primeval and Too Old to Die Young, but it’s hard to pick one or the other because they’re very different.

American Primeval was logistically the hardest project I’ve ever produced and made. We did it for real in the New Mexico desert through winter, spring, summer and fall, with no cover sets and no place to go, with horses and 1800s footwear and clothing, a writers’ strike and a SAG strike. Taylor Kitsch, our lead actor, even broke his foot, and Betty Gilpin, our lead actress, got pregnant during the strikes before having to come back to finish the show. We went from shooting in one winter season with the heaviest snow in New Mexico to finishing the show the next winter season, and it was New Mexico’s warmest winter with no snow.

Too Old to Die Young was the most eccentric creative experience I’ve ever produced. Nick shot 10-minute-long takes where the camera didn’t move. We drove around Hollywood at three in the morning with John Hawkes and Miles Teller. They drove a police car by themselves up the 405 while I was in the backseat with a camera in my hand. A CHP officer followed us and allowed us to do that night after night. It was the most surreal experience.

***The Mosquito Bowl is now streaming on Netflix.

SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#598. Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times."

Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times

The researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times."

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A New Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics."

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

Materials provided by Kyushu University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#597. ‘Twilight’ Director Reveals Robert Pattinson Inspired James Bond Line in 2008 Film: “We Were Seeing the Future”

Earlier this month, it was announced that Pattinson has been tapped as the new 007, succeeding Daniel Craig.

Catherine Hardwicke, who helmed 2008’s Twilight, might as well have had a crystal ball on the set of the vampire romance film.

After it was revealed earlier this month that Robert Pattinson — who earned his breakout role as Edward Cullen in the blockbuster franchise — had been tapped as the new James Bond, fans were quick to point out that Twilight predicted his 007 casting nearly two decades ago.

At one point in the movie, Eric’s (played by Justin Chon) discusses the prom theme and says, “Gambling, tuxedos, and Bond, James Bond,” right before the camera cuts to a smirking Edward, looking suave in a pair of sunglasses. Related Stories Movies Prince Harry Approves of Robert Pattinson's Bond Casting Movies The Time Robert Pattinson Snuck Around Rikers Island (and Why It Could Help Him With James Bond)

Hardwicke also shared her reaction to the news that Pattinson would be going from having “the skin of a killer” to getting his license to kill.

Hardwicke continued to praise The Batman actor’s talents, adding, “He’s intense and interesting and has got a lot of stuff going on in there. He’s weird and he’s original. He does not fit the mold. He’s not afraid to say crazy shit, that’s what I love about it.”

When The Hollywood Reporter caught up with Hardwicke in 2023, ahead of the 15th anniversary of the first Twilight film, she opened up about the challenges of finding the right actor for the role of Edward. She said the actors who were initially auditioning “didn’t look like they’d been alive for almost 100 years and all this deep, soulful angst, existential crisis. However, once Stewart and Pattinson did their chemistry read, the director knew he was the one because she felt “that electricity” between them.

#596. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

#595. FCC Bid Challenging ABC’s TV Licenses Halted in Major Win for Network

The ruling is a major setback for the administration in the government's campaign against ABC and national media.

ABC has won a court order barring the Federal Communications Commission from taking further action against the network amid the government’s efforts to possibly strip the company of its local broadcast licenses.

U.S. District Judge Loren Alikhan on Wednesday rebuffed the FCC‘s bid to dismiss the lawsuit, finding that the agency likely violated ABC’s First Amendment rights by weaponizing its regulatory authority to retaliate against the network for protected speech and pressure it to change its editorial decisions.

“Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration,” an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement. Related Stories TV TV Ratings: 'Dancing With the Stars' Records Another Huge Finale TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Names Historic Season 35 Winner: See All the Scores, Who Won

The Disney-owned company sued the FCC earlier this year after the Brendan Carr-led agency called for an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses. The renewal prompted concerns of retaliation since it followed an investigation into Disney’s diversity practices and ABC late-night host Kimmy Kimmel angering President Donald Trump with a joke.

In Wednesday’s ruling, the court said that Carr’s conduct is “powerful evidence” of the FCC’s “retaliatory motive.”

“It is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings,” Alikhan wrote. She pointed to Carr’s comment that “we can do this the easy way or the hard way” and that “these companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”

The FCC has maintained that the early license renewal proceedings are merely “in aid” of its investigation into Disney’s employment practices and would’ve occurred regardless.

The court was unconvinced, finding that it “does not find that explanation to be credible.” It stressed that Trump has targeted ABC for several years.

The FCC has also launched a separate inquiry into The View, which it argued is not a “bona fide” news program and therefore is not exempt from FCC equal opportunity rules. This came after an appearance by James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for the Texas Senate, in February. ABC said in an earlier filing that the FCC “now appears poised to find that The View must provide equal opportunities to all legally qualified political candidates if it interviews one candidate on the show, which would represent a reversal of decades of agency precedent.”

#594. Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements."

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

For lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly important effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang said. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore."

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds

To test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

The researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

By measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

#591. Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal important details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory

Researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

The researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover new details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Big Bang.

"Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," says Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside."

Du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery

The origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion."

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

He demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

In conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

"Einstein showed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did."

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

The team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

They then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

At first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

"The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis says. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected."

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

Even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

"This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis says. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks."

The discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Big Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

The results also point toward an important characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

Du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas."

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising new approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

The research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.

The House of Mouse, written by longtime Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan, is an unauthorized biography and corporate history of the former Disney CEO that releases Dec. 1. Iger reportedly declined to be interviewed for the book.

In the book, Whelan claimed Iger had an extramarital affair with an ABC marketer in the early 1990s while he was running ABC Entertainment at the time, according to The New York Times, which obtained an advance copy. The relationship was consensual. (Iger was previously married to Susan Iger from 1977 to 1994 and married his current wife, Willow Bay, in 1995.) The woman, who wasn’t identified, became pregnant and “suffered through a traumatic termination procedure,” Mr. Whelan wrote. The Times noted that Whelan contrasts Iger’s personal relationship with his public support for the #MeToo movement in the late 2010s.

Elsewhere in the book, it also claimed the former Disney boss was irritated and vindictive when it came to money. In 2025, Iger received a total compensation package of $45.8 million from the company, an increase from his $41.1 million in 2024, The Hollywood Reporter previously reported.

“I am frustrated about compensation! I had a nasty and distasteful negotiation to extend my contract this last time,” Iger allegedly wrote in a private email in 2014 that was sent to Ike Perlmutter, then Marvel’s chairman and a major Disney shareholder, that Whelan obtained. In 2014, Iger earned $46.5 million, a 36 percent increase from the year prior.

Iger served as Disney CEO twice, first from 2005 to 2020 before he returned in 2022 when Bob Chapek was ousted. Josh D’Amaro took over in March of this year after Iger stepped down.

In The House of Mouse, Iger wasn’t the only Disney exec facing scathing accusations during their time running the company. Whelan also accused Chapek of mocking fans at a Marvel movie premiere in 2022.

The author recounted Chapek gesturing toward fans cosplaying as superheroes and asked, “Did you get a look at the freaks?”

THR reached out to Disney and Iger for comment. The Times reported that Chapek did not respond to their request for comment.

From the skyscrapers of New York to the ancient Parthenon in Athens, the Beaver Moon supermoon put on a spectacular show for skywatchers around the world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.

November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.

Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.

Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in New York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.

Hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of New York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon snapped a series of stunning photos from the International Space Station on Nov. 24, November full moon slipped out of view below Earth's horizon, while being gradually deformed by the warping effect of our planet's atmosphere. "Moonset today from space station - no edits to these photos from 400mm lens," Menon wrote in a post on X.

Heading back down to Earth Salih Zeki Fazlioglu took a colorful photo of the Beaver moon illuminating a thin veil of clouds above Istanbul, Turkiye, as reflected sunlight competed with the artificial glow of the city below for the viewer's attention.

This shot of the lunar disk looming over the Old Post Office Pavillion in Washington D.C. was captured by David Ake, with the pink sky complementing the orange and red leaves of autumn.

Our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.

"Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up."

This striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.

Allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.

"Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image."

Moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?

Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.

That Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.

Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

Feeling inspired to capture your own supermoon photos? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the moon and browse our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography because you don't have long to wait!

The final supermoon of 2026 rises in just a few short weeks on Dec. 23 and it just so happens to be the closest full moon of the year, passing just 221,668 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth at the point of maximum illumination.

So no excuses! We'd love to see your photo in our inbox next month.

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your full moon photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

#588. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

#586. An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.
