#491. Every Disney Easter egg hidden in Hexed

Hexed is flying into cinemas like a teen witch wrangling her newfound magical powers. And if you're concentrating between chaotic cauldron chases, many-eyed monsters, and exploding potions, you'll spy a few Disney Easter eggs in the background.

As Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) explores the magical realm of Hexe with her anxious mother Alice (Rashida Jones) and villainous Queen Celeste (Jodie Foster) on her heels, you might get caught up in all the spectacular sorcery. But if you keep your eyes peeled — all three in familiar Beef Roger Crummchuk's (Walton Goggins) case — you might spot a few references to Disney's animated film catalogue.

So, without spoiling the storyline, here's the Disney references directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand included in Hexed, with some easier to spot than others.

Early in the film (and seen in Hexed teasers), in Billie's room in Ohio, you can easily spot a rug that looks like Aladdin's magic carpet.

Also in Billie's room, on the back of her door, there's a sticker that resembles the Mad Hatter's top hat from Alice In Wonderland.

Painted blue with white crescents and stars, Billie's nail art could be a nod to the Disney sorcerer hat, first worn by Mickey Mouse in Fantasia. There's a related moment in the opening titles of the film, which sees Disney's Steamboat Willie Mickey animation transform into the Fantasia Mickey.

The Little Mermaid's glamorous bargain-maker finds a natural state of entrepreneurship in Hexe's town market, selling deals for "poor unfortunate souls" and showing off her previous customers in macabre jars of seawater.

But wait, this isn't Ursula. She's Cursula, and best of all, she's voiced by Jodi Benson, the icon behind Ariel in The Little Mermaid.

An overt Disney Easter egg that appeared in the trailer, you'll spot the enchanted dancing brooms from Fantasia doing their thing in the middle of the Haven Moon festival in the town square.

When Billie joins a magic class in the Haven Town square (also seen in the Hexed trailer), you can see a nearby tea shop with a sign showing one Mrs Potts from Beauty and the Beast, pouring tea into a teacup that's presumably her precious son, Chip.

When Billie first sees her mother arrive in Hexe (as seen in teasers) you can see a tall blue wizard hat, covered in crescent moons and stars, sitting at a stall. It could be another nod to the Disney sorcerer hat, however, it's accompanied by a long white beard, which suggests it actually belongs to the wizard Merlin from The Sword in the Stone.

Probably the hardest cameos to spot are those of voice actors, but one you might instantly recognise from other Disney films is Alan Tudyk, who plays the Enchanted Sign in Hexe's main town among others. You've heard Tudyk as Frozen's uptight Duke of Weselton, Moana fave Heihei, and Wreck-It Ralph's King Candy.

In a scene where Billie and Alice need to transform into animals, a towel emblazoned with The Little Mermaid's Ariel helps conceal their identities.

It's a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment, and I could be barking up the wrong tree here, but in a scene where Billie quickly passes a group of farmers in a field, a boy lifts his hat to reveal a rat sitting atop his head. If that's not a reference to Ratatouille I'll eat this witch hat.

#489. United Airlines resolves system outage that affected departing flights

United Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.

"We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

A United spokesperson said there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.

The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, said in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights."

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issues that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the issues that caused Friday's ground stop.

— CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Phil LeBeau contributed to this report.

#488. Should Sunrise on the Reaping be the last Hunger Games movie?

The Hunger Games has never been more back.

Over its opening weekend, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping topped the domestic box office with an impressive $120 million, making it just one of five movies to open with over $100 million this year. Other titles to achieve that goal are Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Toy Story 5, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, and The Odyssey.

With Sunrise on the Reaping's massive success comes questions about the future of the franchise. What could our next trip to Panem look like? Which character could author Suzanne Collins focus on in a new novel? Oft-floated options include fan-favorite victor Finnick Odair (Sam Claflin), which would give audiences a look at a Career's experience in the Hunger Games, or Gamemaker Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), which would offer a different perspective on the rebellion against President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

Alternatively, what if we just let the franchise rest for a little longer? That seems to be the plan for now, as Lionsgate chairman Adam Fogelson told Variety that there would be no more new films until Collins wrote another book. And honestly, if Collins chooses to move on from Panem forever, would that be so awful? The Hunger Games has proven it has staying power, but with Sunrise on the Reaping, it's also begun to show the limits of the books' formula. Not that Sunrise on the Reaping is bad — far from it! However, it does make a pretty solid case as to why it should be the franchise's closer.

When Collins first announced the release of Sunrise on the Reaping, I was skeptical. Film audiences already knew how Haymitch Abernathy's (Joseph Zada) games would end. Book readers had even seen it play out in an abridged version on the page in Catching Fire, when Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) watched it to prepare for the Third Quarter Quell.

Still, Collins proved me wrong. The novel deepened our understanding of the Capitol's propaganda machine, revealing that the version of Haymitch's games that Katniss and Peeta watched was edited to omit Haymitch's attempt to break the arena. It also emphasized that characters from the original trilogy like Haymitch, Plutarch, Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke) had all been working to undermine Snow since before Katniss was even born. Yes, their sparks of rebellion didn't catch fire at first. But we know that they eventually build and build until Snow is overthrown in Mockingjay. By the end of the book, Haymitch lives to see the sun rise on his birthday with no reaping in site, adding a bittersweet layer to the hard-fought tragedy of his games.

Sunrise on the Reaping, both the film and the novel, closes with the return of Katniss and Peeta, now grown up. Their appearance brings Sunrise on the Reaping full circle, looking to Panem's future while also deepening our understanding of its past. Do we really need to break that circle open again when Collins has already written such a meaningful conclusion?

My biggest complaint about the book and film versions of Sunrise on the Reaping is the same: They both suffer from prequel-itis. That's when a prequel is so focused on linking back to the original title that it becomes bogged down in references and callbacks. In Sunrise on the Reaping's case, that prequel-itis manifests in the nonstop barrage of returning characters, whose presence can almost suffocate the new characters. Collins still weaves a compelling story of rebellion with them, but by the time young Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning) showed up, I almost rolled my eyes at how connected everything was.

If Collins returns to Panem to tell the story of a known character like Finnick or Plutarch, it's possible that novel would suffer a similar fate. The world of the series would grow ever smaller, instead of expanding. Collins could also opt to avoid the Hunger Games entirely and focus instead on the Dark Days before the Capitol created the Games. But without the spectacle of the Hunger Games themselves, how can Lionsgate expect audiences to show up? After all, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes only featured a rudimentary version of the Hunger Games, and it took in $44 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend, a little over a third of Sunrise on the Reaping's total. The disparity proves that people want to see the Hunger Games on a large scale, preferably with familiar faces. But when it comes to storytelling, those desires might wind up being greater flaws than boons in the long run.

Again, Collins proved my skepticism about Sunrise on the Reaping dead wrong, and I'd like to think that she truly won't write another Hunger Games novel unless she has something new and compelling to say. But given that Sunrise on the Reaping serves as such a fitting bookend to the original trilogy, and that it's beginning to show the warning signs of franchise fatigue, it might be best to let it stand as a strong conclusion, as opposed to a gateway for further meddling in a well-trodden story.

#486. Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports

According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

#484. Centuries-old dust hints at a dying stars last-minute chaos

The mix of elements that ends up in planets — even people — can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star, new space observations suggest.

A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A, a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star. Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, the astronomers could parse out clumps within the 350-year-old cloud and analyze their compositions. The debris from the explosion, called a supernova, is still racing outward in space at about 11 million mph.

"What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," said Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement.

Supernova explosions forge and scatter many of the heavy elements that later get recycled into new stars and worlds. Computer models have long predicted that a star's inner layers could merge before it explodes. But scientists don't fully understand why and how some stars go through this violent process. The new study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds evidence that it happened in Cassiopeia A, giving astronomers a way to peer inside a star that hasn't existed for centuries.

A massive star builds up in layers, like an onion, with each shell fusing a different element. When the star explodes, some of that material cools into dust. Each layer makes its own kind of dust, so the grains, smaller than the width of a human hair, keep a record of what sat where inside the star.

As the layers merge, they can change the mix of elements the blast flings out, said Tea Temim, lead author of the study.

"So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly," said Temim, a research scientist at Columbia University in New York. "And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion."

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Light Speed newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

To look for evidence, the team pointed Webb at three spots in Cassiopeia A, or Cas A, that NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope had previously flagged. Spitzer saw the debris as a blur, with light from many clumps mixed together. Webb's sharper view separates individual clumps, each roughly the size of our solar system, so the team could study them one at a time.

One clump held mostly silica dust, the main ingredient in most sand. Another held mostly carbon dust. The third sits in a feature nicknamed the Green Monster, and its dust is rich in magnesium and silicon. That material didn't come from the blast at all; rather, the star shed it before it exploded.

The researchers then compared their measurements with existing computer models of exploding stars. Only the models in which the star's layers had merged could reproduce both the silica-rich and the carbon-rich debris. A wider Webb dust map shows signs of the merger across much of the cloud.

The team cautions that those models are incomplete. Researchers will need more detailed 3D simulations — and Webb observations of more spots in the cloud — to confirm the merger.

This approach also could help astronomers make sense of supernovas in other galaxies.

"I think it's remarkable that we can watch these changes and understand what they mean from thousands of light-years away," Milisavljevic said.

#483. This Hollywood Star Took on Crypto. Now He’s Got a New Target

Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous. At the end of his documentary taking on the cryptocurrency industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money,” the former star of The O.C. and Gotham turned to his spouse and fellow actor Morena Baccarin and swore he was done.

Turns out, that scene might need an edit. McKenzie is launching a new nonprofit, The Public Trust and Transparency Project, that not only continues his battle with the crypto business but widens it to fight prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi.

McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.”

“The more gambling gets into our culture, the more people feel like it's somehow a good idea to view these things as legitimate investment strategies,” he says. The prediction markets reject the comparison (although 80 percent of Kalshi’s trades came from sports in September, according to Bloomberg). McKenzie rejects the rejection: “I mean, if your investment strategy is, ‘I'm going to gamble on the Spurs-Knicks,’ like, come on! So there's a real, real problem here.”

John Reed Stark, who spent 18 years in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s enforcement division, will serve as an adviser to the Project. American Kleptocracy author Casey Michel and Tonantzin Carmona, who runs economic policy for the left-of-center Century Foundation, will sit on the board.

The group is coming together at a time when regulators and law enforcement officials at every level are looking to rein in prediction markets. Federal regulators have launched new probes into both major prediction markets. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee recently released its investigation into US troops and government insiders trading on insider knowledge on Polymarket and Kalshi. The Senate just passed a bill prohibiting prediction markets for military operations and assassinations. Executives at the markets know they’re in for a rough few months; Kalshi even launched an ad campaign, starring Martha Stewart, reminding its users not to trade on confidential information.

But insider trading is only one concern among many. There’s also the problem you find in old-school gambling houses too: The vast majority of people who use the markets lose their money. A recent Wall Street Journal report shows that .01 percent of accounts take in two-thirds of all of the profits on Polymarket. On Kalshi, unprofitable accounts outpace profitable ones by almost three to one.

Then there’s the corruption angle, which McKenzie says is going to be front-and-center for the Project, especially with it featuring as a top issue in the recent midterm elections. Donald Trump Jr. was, until recently, a paid adviser to Kalshi. Trump Jr.’s venture firm, 1789 Capital, made its latest and biggest in a series of investments in Polymarket over the summer; months earlier, the Trump Justice Department sued the state of Minnesota when it tried to ban the prediction markets in the state. (At a recent conference, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called Trump Jr.’s involvement “heavily overblown. We have all types of investors.”)

Prediction markets have been around for hundreds of years, as a forthcoming book on the subject notes. American academics have been turning to them as teaching tools since the late ’80s. Their advocates note that they can be an effective way to hedge against risk, and a form of trading on sports that’s far more consumer-friendly than the online gambling houses. “I accept that there may be some utility,” McKenzie notes. “I'm not saying these things should not exist. I'm just saying they need to be properly regulated.”

McKenzie’s plan will be to push Congress in that direction, sort of the inverse of how the former actor lobbied publicly and privately against the “Clarity Act,” which would’ve brought cryptocurrencies into the financial mainstream. (The bill was rejected in September.)

That pressure is only bound to increase when Democrats take control of Congress next year. “In the bold new world starting [on the] first Monday in January,” Representative Frank Lucas, an Oklahoma Republican, told Politico, “nobody’s untouchable anymore.”

#481. The Rings of Power cast on Sauron and Celeborns kiss, Gandalfs hat, and the forging of the One Ring

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 wraps up today, and what a season it has been.

Season 3 teased the Witch-king of Angmar. It pulled deep from J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium to reveal the Dark Wizard's (Ciarán Hinds) true identity. It introduced Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) and promptly flung him into Sauron's (Charlie Vickers) torture chamber. But most importantly, this season saw the forging of the almighty One Ring in the fires of Mount Doom.

In a Say More interview with Mashable Entertainment Reporter Belen Edwards, cast members Vickers, Bower, Cynthia Addai-Robinson, and Daniel Weyman, as well as series co-creator Patrick McKay, broke down pivotal moments from the season, starting with the One Ring's forging.

"It was two weeks of hammering," Vickers joked of filming the scene.

Extensive hammering aside, the sequence is a fiery symphony in which Sauron gives himself wholly to dark creation. Lava-drenched and menacing, it's wholly unlike the forging of any of the other rings of power we've seen onscreen in the series so far. For showrunners McKay and J.D. Payne, that was the goal.

"We wanted it to be more than he's making a weapon or a magical object," McKay said. "He's changing as a character forever. The world is changing in this moment."

In the interview, Bower and Vickers also discussed Sauron and Celeborn's surprise kiss. Plus, Robinson dug into Míriel's decision to marry Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle). Be sure to stick around until the end for Weyman's moving discussion of what it means for Gandalf to don his iconic hat for the first time. It may leave your eyes mistier than the Misty Mountains.

#479. FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?

Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?

Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.

Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.

Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.

He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.

"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."

Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.

The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.

During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.

"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.

"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.

But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.

"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he said.

"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.

However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.

If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

#478. Zelda Switch 2 restock: Live restock updates at Walmart, Target, and Best Buy (Nov. 25)

If your current morning ritual involves violently hitting refresh on a dozen retail tabs, you already know the vibe: finding the Nintendo Switch 2: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition is turning into an Olympic sport.

We're closely monitoring inventory at all the major retailers and are cautiously optimistic it will be restocked for the holiday shopping season. On the question of if/when the limited-edition Zelda Switch 2 will be restocked, a Nintendo spokesperson provided this not-entirely-reassuring statement to Mashable: "Although we cannot provide detailed information, we are striving to ensure that we can supply our products to those who want them."

Between automated bot armies scooping digital drops, surprise order cancellations at Walmart, and inventory vanishing in seconds on Amazon, this custom black-and-gold console feels like a myth. But while digital storefronts look completely barren, stock is actively circulating behind the scenes.

Before getting into the restock details, bookmark these retailer pages to check for surprise drops:

Nintendo Store — Out of stock right now, but you can add it to your wishlist to get pinged the second a restock hits.

Amazon — Dropping tiny batches of consoles randomly throughout the day.

Walmart — Stock exists but only for third-party listings selling at way over market price, so make sure your in-stock email alerts are turned on.

Target — Sold out online, but periodic drops have taken place in-store.

Best Buy — Sold out online, but select stores ran midnight openings on Nov. 5 with walk-in stock.

GameStop — Online orders are off; you will have to walk into a store to find one.

The feeding frenzy is being supercharged by Nintendo’s staggered release calendar. While the custom Zelda 40th Anniversary hardware dropped first on Oct. 29, the flagship game driving demand — The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 — arrived on Thursday, Nov. 5.

The remake rebuilds the 1998 classic from the ground up with modernized controls, a fully orchestrated soundtrack, reworked dungeon puzzles, and expanded Hyrule environments. Since the $520 console doesn’t include the game, everyone is rushing to lock down a system before launch day.

The package includes the special-edition Switch 2 system sporting a custom black-and-gold finish, themed Joy-Con 2 controllers, and a matching dock decorated with the gold Triforce emblem. It retains the platform's signature flexibility, letting you switch between TV, Tabletop, and Handheld modes whenever you want. Inside the themed chassis, you get 256GB of built-in storage (expandable with microSD Express cards), a vivid display in handheld mode, faster load times, and support for up to 4K resolution on compatible TVs when the console sits in the dock.

The magnetic Joy-Con 2 controllers add mouse-style tracking in supported games, while the new GameChat hub lets you voice chat and share your screen directly as you play. It also plays your older Switch games and supports standard multiplayer options.

Landing limited-edition Nintendo hardware takes a little prep work, but these battle-tested habits will give you a real edge over the bots:

Save your checkout details everywhere — Log in to Target, Best Buy, Walmart, and the Nintendo Store to save your shipping address and default card. Stopping to type a card number or billing zip code during a live drop is how you lose an order.

Hands off the refresh button in Best Buy's queue — When an online drop goes live, Best Buy puts shoppers into a randomized waiting line to filter out scrapers. Touching the reload button resets your spot and boots you straight to the back.

Watch for Walmart+ early-access paywalls — Walmart frequently locks headline console drops behind paid Walmart+ subscriptions for the first 30 to 60 minutes. If you have a membership, keep that tab signed in; if not, wait for the general public window to unlock.

Dodge third-party sellers — Double-check the seller before buying. Marketplace scalpers frequently list units for jacked-up prices; make sure it says "Sold and shipped by [Retailer]" at the standard price.

Skip the web wars and head to physical stores — Online checkout bots grab website stock in under 15 seconds. Showing up in person is easily your most reliable path to securing one without paying scalper markups.

Hopefully, yes, but this hasn't been confirmed.

Stores like Walmart, Amazon, and Best Buy often hold onto popular gaming hardware to use as headline deals during Black Friday and Cyber Monday week.

With that said, Black Friday restocks are usually the hardest ones to catch. You will be fighting website crashes, gift shoppers, and automated bots all at once. If you can grab a console whenever stock appears, take it. Think of Black Friday as a backup plan, not your main bet.

Console hunting sucks right now, period. But between the surprise micro-drops and physical store restocks, you still have real shots at retail price — just be ready to move the second that stock goes live.
